What is Apache Ignite?

1. What is Apache Ignite?
  • Apache Ignite is an open-source distributed database for high-performance computing with in-memory speed;
  • It stores data across a cluster of nodes in RAM (and optionally on disk), providing microsecond-level latency for reads and writes;
  • It is not just a cache — it is a full-fledged distributed database that supports SQL, key-value operations, compute, and more;
2. Why is Apache Ignite needed?
  • Performance — traditional databases store data on disk; when traffic spikes, disk I/O becomes the bottleneck; Ignite stores data in RAM, which is orders of magnitude faster;
  • Scalability — data is automatically partitioned and distributed across all cluster nodes; adding nodes increases both storage capacity and throughput linearly;
  • Reducing database load — Ignite can sit between your application and a relational database, serving reads from memory and writing through to the DB, dramatically reducing load on the primary database;
  • Real-time processing — use cases that demand sub-millisecond response times (fraud detection, trading systems, IoT telemetry) benefit from Ignite's memory-first architecture;
3. What are the core capabilities?
  • Distributed Key-Value Store — store and retrieve data using key-value pairs with ACID transaction support;
  • Distributed SQL — execute ANSI SQL queries across the distributed dataset, including joins, aggregations, and DML;
  • Distributed Compute — execute arbitrary Java code (closures, tasks) on cluster nodes where the data resides, eliminating network overhead;
  • Native Persistence — optionally persist data to disk so the cluster survives full restarts without data loss;
  • Machine Learning — train ML models directly on data stored in Ignite without ETL to external systems;
  • Continuous Queries — receive real-time notifications when data in the cache changes;
  • Services — deploy singleton or per-node services that are automatically redeployed on failover;
4. How is Ignite different from Redis, Memcached, and Hazelcast?
Feature Apache Ignite Redis Memcached Hazelcast
Distributed SQL Full ANSI SQL with joins Limited (modules) No SQL-like (Jet)
ACID Transactions Yes (cross-partition) Single-key only No Yes
Native Persistence Yes (disk + memory tiers) RDB/AOF snapshots No Hot Restart (Enterprise)
Compute Grid Yes (collocated compute) Lua scripting No Yes
Machine Learning Built-in ML library No No No
Data Partitioning Automatic (affinity-based) Manual (cluster mode) Client-side Automatic
5. Key Terms
  • Cluster — a group of interconnected Ignite nodes that share data and computation;
  • Server Node — stores data in memory (and optionally on disk), executes compute tasks, and processes SQL queries;
  • Client Node — joins the cluster topology but does not store data; used to stream data in or execute queries;
  • Thin Client — a lightweight client that connects to the cluster over TCP without joining the topology; available in Java, .NET, Python, Node.JS, C++;
  • Cache — a named key-value data structure distributed across the cluster; equivalent to a SQL table;
  • Partition — a subset of the data set; Ignite divides each cache into 1024 partitions by default, distributed evenly across server nodes;
  • Affinity — the function that maps a key to a specific partition (and therefore to a specific node);
  • Backup — a copy of a partition stored on a different node for fault tolerance;
  • Baseline Topology — the set of server nodes that persists data; determines which nodes participate in data storage;
